ceviri.33: What exactly is SEO-friendly web design?
ceviri.34: SEO-friendly design is an approach that aims for a page to be both understood by the search engine and easy for the visitor to use. The order of the layout, the heading hierarchy, the visual weight and the mobile behaviour are its four main decisions. Rather than squeezing the text into the page afterwards, it puts the content at the centre of the design. The visitor finds what they're looking for faster, stays on the page longer, and is more likely to get in touch. We work that structure out separately for every project; we don't proceed on a ready-made template.
ceviri.35: Can I improve visibility without having my current site rebuilt?
ceviri.36: Yes, you can. On most projects we tidy the homepage layout and the heading order first. Then we go over the mobile view. Those two interventions make a visible difference while keeping the existing infrastructure. We assess the decision on a full rebuild together at the next stage.
ceviri.37: Is a layout change more important than the content?
ceviri.38: The two complete each other; they don't compete. Weak content isn't rescued by a good layout, and strong content stays invisible in a bad one. In practice we write the content first and build the layout around it. When the order runs that way, both sides win.
ceviri.39: Which sections cause the most trouble at the mobile breakpoint?
ceviri.40: Menus, tables and multi-column sections are the areas that struggle most on a narrow screen. We turn the menu into a plain structure that opens with a single tap. We move tables into a card view rather than horizontal scrolling. We stack the columns and set the order by importance.
ceviri.41: Do we have to reduce the number of images?
ceviri.42: No — what matters is function, not number. Every image should have a job on the page: showing the product, explaining the process, or building trust. We take out the images with no job. The ones that stay we place at the right size and in the right format.
ceviri.43: How long does the design process take?
ceviri.44: It varies with scope. Single-page promotional sites are finished in a few weeks. On multi-section corporate projects the timeline lengthens. We settle the schedule at the discovery stage and share the delivery date for each step in writing.
ceviri.45: Are template themes enough for this?
ceviri.46: Templates do a job to start with, but they limit you in the long run. Off-the-shelf themes usually carry a lot of sections and unnecessary images. Cleaning those out can take longer than building from scratch. Once the brand narrative is clear, a bespoke structure stays more flexible.
ceviri.47: Does a design change affect rankings straight away?
ceviri.48: No, the effect usually becomes clear within a few weeks. It takes time for the new layout to show up in visitor behaviour. Patient measurement is essential.

ceviri.62: How Does SEO-Friendly Web Design Affect Search Visibility?
ceviri.63: Showing up in the search results isn't a question of text alone. The moment a visitor lands on a page they make a decision: stay, or go back. The design largely makes that decision for them. SEO-friendly web design is the approach that brings the structure a search engine understands together with the order a person understands. On SME projects we build those two sides at the same table. Through this piece we'll talk about layout, visual weight and mobile breakpoint decisions.
ceviri.64: Design decisions set the order in which the content is seen.
ceviri.66: Which Design Decisions Touch the Rankings?
ceviri.67: Design decisions affect search visibility indirectly, but powerfully. The search engine reads the content; the visitor reads the layout. When the two contradict each other, the ranking drops. The layout, the heading order and the use of white space set how much of the content actually gets seen. That's why we take the design and the content decisions in the same meeting.
ceviri.68: A page's value lies in the text for the search engine, and in the first glance for the visitor. SEO-friendly web design brings those two values together in one structure. The menu gets simpler, the headings fall into order, and the important content moves up. That's why we talk about the SEO side of the design at the first draft.
ceviri.69: We handle measurement topics such as crawling and indexing separately; that side falls within the scope of our
ceviri.72: SEO-friendly web design starts from this fact: the visitor doesn't read the page, they scan it. Their eye stops on headings, buttons and bold phrases. When the design makes that scanning habit easier, the content gets the attention it deserves. Otherwise even well-written text goes to waste.
ceviri.73: The story the design tells the search engine
ceviri.74: A search engine doesn't feel the appearance of a page directly. It still draws a meaning from the heading order, the link structure and the order of the content. A tidy interface presents the subject with a clear hierarchy. A scattered one weakens the signal.
ceviri.75: The link between user behaviour and design
ceviri.76: If a visitor can't find what they're after, they go back. That return is a behaviour showing the page didn't meet the question. A well-built layout carries the answer to the first screen. Time on page lengthens, and the page holds its place in the search results. Where the answer sits is as decisive as the answer itself.
ceviri.77: What Does Page Layout Mean in Search?
ceviri.78: Page layout is the order that sets in which sequence and with what weight the content is presented. On the search side, that order raises the clarity of the subject. On the visitor side, it shortens the decision time. A design that pushes an important heading down can make even strong text invisible. The layout drawing doesn't start before the content plan is ready.
ceviri.79: The mistake we see most often on corporate pages is every section being designed with equal weight. On a page like that, no message stands out. Yet SEO alignment in web design starts with making the priority visible. And we set the order of priority by the first question the client asks.
ceviri.80: We pick a single main message. We put it on the first screen.

ceviri.84: There is only one H1 on a page; below it come the H2 blocks that divide the subject, and beneath those the supporting subheadings. In SEO-friendly web design practice, when that order breaks, both the visitor and the search engine lose the thread. We number the headings before we write them.
ceviri.85: What should be visible on the first screen?
ceviri.86: The first screen is the area visible when the page opens, without scrolling. We put three things there: what we do, who it helps, and a link to act on. The rest goes below. That simplicity speeds up both reading and conversion.
ceviri.88: White space isn't decoration. The breathing room between two sections sets the reading order. On cramped pages the headings blur into each other and the reader doesn't know where to stop. We open the gaps between sections to a fixed measure, so every heading owns its own text.
ceviri.90: Yes, visual weight affects rankings. Enormous cover images push the text down. The visitor sees the message late and runs out of patience early. When we position an image as part of the story rather than as decoration, both readability and visibility gain. An image doesn't replace the text; it supports it. We make that distinction section by section.

ceviri.94: Every image should answer a question. Is it showing the product, explaining the process, or building trust? If there's no answer, we remove the image. In SEO-friendly web design decisions, white space does as much work as an image; when we take a box out, we make room for text. We place the images that remain at the right size, with page speed in mind.
ceviri.95: Visual density and the balance with content
ceviri.96: Images and text on a page should feed each other. In practice we follow a simple balance rule: at most one strong image per main section. We break the text blocks at three or four lines. The eye doesn't tire while scrolling, and the message settles piece by piece.
ceviri.98: Light grey text on grey looks elegant and can't be read on a phone in daylight. The first of the SEO-friendly web design decisions is legibility; the colour palette doesn't drop below that limit. We keep the brand colours and leave the body text in a dark tone.
ceviri.99: What do we put in place of an image?
ceviri.100: When a section is left without an image, we don't go looking for decoration. Most of the time a short three-item list or a clear subheading does the same job. Those are read, and they reach the search engine as text. We use a cover image only where it can explain the subject at a glance.
ceviri.101: What Do We Watch at the Mobile Breakpoints?
ceviri.102: Our first rule at the mobile breakpoint is simple: content isn't lost, it's only rearranged. The breakpoint is the threshold at which the design is rearranged according to the width of the screen. A layout that looks fine on a desktop can become unreadable on a narrow screen. That's why we start the design from the phone screen. We settle the breakpoints before coding begins. That way surprise corrections disappear.
ceviri.103: Three things break on a narrow screen: the menu, the tables and the multi-column sections. Our checklist is short and numerical.
ceviri.104: Touch targets should be at least 44 pixels high.
ceviri.105: Body text shouldn't drop below 16 pixels.
ceviri.106: The main call-to-action button should be visible on the first scroll.
ceviri.107: No section should produce horizontal scrolling.
ceviri.108: We follow the public data on how widespread mobile use is through
ceviri.110: — BTK is Türkiye's information and communication technologies authority. That's why we draw the wireframe at the narrow screen width first and then open it out to the desktop. When the order is reversed, menus overflow and tables scroll sideways.
ceviri.111: We handle the mobile equivalent of the interface decisions with the same logic in
ceviri.113: . We put the breakpoint thresholds in writing at the start of the project.
ceviri.115: On a phone there is no clicking, there is tapping. When small links are lined up next to each other, the finger finds the wrong target. We enlarge the buttons and put space between them. The complaint about mis-taps doesn't come in after that adjustment.
ceviri.117: The mobile version should carry the same information as the desktop. In a search-friendly design approach that equality isn't up for negotiation. Some agencies hide sections on a narrow screen; we don't hide them, we fold them. The visitor opens them if they want to and moves on if they don't. That way the story the page tells stays whole on every device.

ceviri.120: Get a Quote for SEO-Friendly Web Design
ceviri.121: We start the quote process with a discovery meeting and put the layout wireframe to you for approval. The goal, the content inventory and the competitor pages come to the table on day one. Once approval comes through, the design and the coding move forward. We share the reasoning behind every decision in writing. That way the budget rests on a plan rather than a guess. If you have an existing site, we look at that too.
ceviri.122: The success of a design project is measured not on delivery day but in the third month. That's why we stay with you after launch as well. In the first months we follow visitor behaviour and suggest small corrections to the layout.

_kararlar.mobil kırılım noktası → mobile breakpoin: İkisi de sektörün İngilizce terimleri; 'content parity' mobil/masaüstü eşitliği için standart ifade.
_kararlar.ilk ekran → the first screen: Türkçe metin terimi zaten tanımlıyor ('kaydırma yapmadan görünen alan'). Tabloda ise 'ekranın altına iner' geçtiği için orada 'below the fold' kullanıldı — İngilizcede o deyim tabloya daha iyi oturuyor.
_kararlar.109/110 BTK: EN-DEVAM'daki Türk kurumları desenine eklendi: bağlantı metni kısa ('BTK's publications'), açıklama sonraki kayda taşındı ('Türkiye's information and communication technologies authority').
